title: Small among my brothers
sum: David speaks of himself. He was the small one, the youngest, keeping his father's sheep; his hands made instruments and his fingers tuned a harp (1:1–2). Who would tell the Lord about him? The Lord himself heard (1:3). God sent his messenger, took him from the sheep and anointed him; his tall, handsome brothers were passed over (1:4–5). Then he went out against the Philistine who cursed him by his idols, drew the giant's own sword, cut off his head, and lifted the shame from Israel (1:6–7). The whole story of 1 Samuel 16–17 is here in seven verses.

The Greek heading calls it David's psalm "in his own hand" but "outside the number," not one of the 150. A longer Hebrew form, in two poems, was found in the Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11Q5), and comparing the two shows how the Greek shortened and sometimes blurred its source (1:3). The Orthodox and Coptic churches keep it in their Psalters; Catholics and Protestants count 150 psalms.
readings: Taken as the heading presents it, the psalm is David looking back from the day of Goliath on God's strange choice of him. It agrees with 1 Samuel at every point it touches, except that it calls God's messenger an "angel" (1:4).
Read as a retelling of 1 Samuel

Read beside 1 Samuel 16–17, it is a short poem that gathers the story's key words: smallest, shepherd, lyre, anointed among his brothers, not the tall ones, curses by his gods, the sword, the shame lifted. The Hebrew in 11Q5 is fuller, and Sanders took it as the source of the Greek.
Read as a psalm of the chosen small one
A Christian reader can set it beside God's habit of choosing what the world counts weak (1 Corinthians 1:27) and beside the shepherd king whose greater son is Jesus.

views.O: Orthodox Psalters print the psalm after Psalm 150 with its heading, "not numbered with the one hundred and fifty psalms" (Asser's Psalter, 2005). An Orthodox parish answer says it "has never been considered part of the body of the Psalms themselves," while keeping it in the Psalter book. For the Coptic Orthodox, a church site says the psalm is read every year on Bright Saturday, the day before the feast of the Resurrection.
views.H: The psalm is a short poem built on 1 Samuel 16–17. Its Hebrew form in 11Q5, a Psalms Scroll from Qumran, has two poems (151A and 151B) and reads more clearly than the Greek; Sanders explained the Greek as a shortened translation of a Hebrew text like it, a view Wikipedia's "Psalm 151" says scholars now accept; before 11Q5 the psalm was held to be composed in Greek. One possible reading is that the heading's claim of David's own hand vouches for an extra psalm.
views.J: The psalm is not in the Jewish Bible, whose Psalter has 150 psalms. Before the Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11Q5) was found in 1956, no Hebrew text of it was known, where it stands after other compositions about David, among them a prose note that David wrote 3,600 psalms and 450 songs, 4,050 in all, "through prophecy" given him "from before the Most High." A scroll copied about AD 30–50 thus carries psalms of David beyond the 150; scholars differ on whether it is a variant edition of the Psalter or a collection for worship drawn from it (Wikipedia, "Great Psalms Scroll").
views.N: Two links with the New Testament are echoes of the larger story, not quotations. David the shepherd anointed in Bethlehem stands behind the shepherds who hear of a Savior born "in David's town" (Luke 2:8–11) and behind "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11). God "took no delight" in the tall brothers (1:5) with the verb the voice from heaven uses of Jesus, "in you I take delight" (Luke 3:22).
views.W: Western churches count 150 psalms: the Council of Trent defined "the Davidical Psalter, consisting of a hundred and fifty psalms," and Protestant Bibles follow the Hebrew Psalter. The psalm is not even in the Apocrypha of the KJV or in the list of Article VI. Western readers meet it as a witness to how David's story was sung, read beside 1 Samuel.

deep.b:
The Psalms Scroll from Qumran Cave 11 (11Q5) gathers biblical psalms with other poems, and near its end it has two Hebrew poems that match the Greek Psalm 151. In the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription (ETCBC) they are in the column numbered 28, lines 3 to 14. The first (151A) is headed "Hallelujah. Of David son of Jesse" and runs from David's youth to his anointing; the second (151B) is headed "The beginning of David's mighty deeds after the prophet of God had anointed him" and breaks off as he sees "a Philistine taunting from the ranks of the Philistines." Just before them, the scroll has a prose note: David was "wise" and "a scribe," and the LORD gave him "a spirit of understanding and light," so that he wrote 3,600 psalms, and songs to sing before the altar: 364 for the daily offering, one for each day of the year, and further songs for Sabbaths, new moons and festivals (450 songs in all), 4,050 compositions in all, "through prophecy" given him "from before the Most High."

Set side by side, the Hebrew is longer and clearer. The Greek's puzzling 1:3, "who will tell my Lord?", stands where the Hebrew has "who can tell ... the deeds of the Lord?" The Greek "angel" stands where the Hebrew has "his prophet ... Samuel." The Greek has one psalm where the scroll has two; the Goliath poem breaks off in the scroll after about two lines, so the Greek's last verses cannot be compared with it. In the Hebrew line behind 1:3 the transcription ends a sentence after "the Lord" and marks one letter as uncertain, so that line can be read more than one way (see the variant at 1:3).

The Hebrew Psalter has 150 psalms, and so do the Catholic and Protestant Bibles (the Council of Trent's decree says "a hundred and fifty psalms"). The Greek Psalter has the same 150, numbered a little differently, and then this one, which its own heading puts "outside the number." The manuscripts reflect the doubt: Swete's notes give Codex Sinaiticus's subscription as "151 psalms of David," while Codex Alexandrinus counts 150 and adds the extra psalm separately; in the Verona Psalter a later hand added it (Swete, Introduction). So the psalm has always been both in the Psalter book and outside its count.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the shortest telling of 1 Samuel 16:7
deep.b: 1 Samuel 16:7 gives the rule of the whole David story: "A human sees what is before the eyes, but the LORD sees the heart." Psalm 151 is that verse turned into a life. Each half of the psalm sets an outward measure against God's choice: small against big brothers (1:1, 1:5), a boy's homemade music against a messenger from God (1:2–4), a giant's curses by his idols against a boy who takes his sword (1:6–7). One way to read the hard line, "who will tell my Lord? The Lord himself, he himself listens" (1:3), fits this: no human report recommended David; God heard for himself. This is Claude's own reading.

echoes: 1 Samuel 16:1–13; 1 Samuel 16:16–23; 1 Samuel 17:4–51; Psalm 78:70–72; Psalm 89:20; Psalm 144:1; Genesis 4:21; 2 Samuel 7:8; Luke 2:8–11; Luke 3:22; John 10:11

settings.what: Psalm 151, David's song of his choosing and his victory
settings.by: David, as the heading presents him ("in David's own hand")
settings.to: the hearers of the psalm, and God, who "listens" (1:3)
settings.when: the heading sets it at the duel with Goliath (1 Samuel 17); its content looks back over the anointing (1 Samuel 16) as well
settings.why: To praise God for choosing the small one: the youngest son, a shepherd and musician, overlooked beside his tall brothers but chosen by God, anointed, and given victory over the giant who mocked Israel. The psalm puts the lesson of 1 Samuel 16:7 in David's own mouth.
settings.readers: The community whose library held 11Q5, which places the psalm near its end, just after a prose list of the thousands of songs David wrote "through prophecy" (what the scroll was for is debated); then Greek-speaking Jews and Christians who read it after Psalm 150 in the Greek Psalter. Who first wrote it is unknown.
views: The heading claims it, and Orthodox Psalters print it as David's, though "outside the number."

The psalm is built from 1 Samuel 16–17 and, in Hebrew, survives first in a scroll from Qumran that gathers David's songs; a later poet may have written it to give David's voice to his own story, as the prose note before it in 11Q5 credits David with 4,050 songs.
